2028 Volkswagen Golf R To Feature Twincharged 2.0 TSI Mild-Hybrid Powertrain From T-Roc R
7 photos
Photo: Volkswagen
The largest European automaker of them all is preparing a powertrain update for its flagship hatchback, which can also be had as a family-oriented longroof. Come summer 2027 for model year 2028, the Golf R should gain the e-charger and variable-geometry turbo from the newly redesigned T-Roc R crossover, bringing a different approach to torque delivery while complying with Euro 7 regs.
Reinhold Ivenz, namely the head of the R go-faster division, suggested the upcoming change to British motoring publication Auto Express during the launch of the 2027 model year T-Roc R . According to Ivenz, the Golf R will pack a bigger punch from lower engine speeds, improving acceleration from a standing start.
Considering the well-known oversimplification that puts torque ahead of horsepower, that certainly sounds like more torque earlier in the rev range. Truth be told, horsepower actually governs both acceleration and top speed. Gearing may let you trade engine speed for twisting force at the wheels, but a transmission does not multiply horsepower.
Having made that clear, a twincharged engine has an inherent advantage over using only a turbocharger. Exhaust-driven turbos are usually bad at producing instant boost before exhaust gases build up, creating turbo lag while requiring more revs to deliver maximum torque and power.
The electric supercharger in the T-Roc R, which is more efficient than Volvo's belt-driven Eaton TVS Roots-type blower, uses the 48-volt system to compress intake air before the exhaust-gas turbocharger wakes up.
Filling the boost gap results in 420 Newton-meters (310 pound-feet) from 1,900 revolutions per minute compared to 2,100 for the outgoing Golf R, peak torque that stays relatively flat until the tacho reads 5,250 revolutions per minute. Peak power arrives 150 revs later, at 5,750 instead of 5,600 revolutions per minute, because torque starts tapering off earlier in the rev range.
Photo: Volkswagen Volkswagen calls these mills EA888 evo4 in the Golf R's case, and EA888 evo5 in the T-Roc R. Both make 333 ps (328 hp) at full chatter, and both rely on iron blocks for extra strength. To recap, two compressors perform complementary jobs in the new-gen engine. The electrically-driven unit supports low-speed grunt while the VTG-type turbo supplies the airflow needed as both engine load and exhaust flow increase.
To satisfy Euro 7 regulations, the EA888 evo5 further benefits from a direct fuel injection system that operates at up to 500 bar instead of 350 bar. The 150-bar jump atomizes the dinosaur juice into a finer mist, improving combustion efficiency while increasing knock resistance under high boost.
Volkswagen also uses the Miller cycle, which closes the intake valves early during the intake stroke to cool the trapped air inside the cylinders before compression starts. The expanded and cooled air drops combustion temperatures, which is way more efficient than dumping excess fuel into the cylinders. In the T-Roc R, the combustion system is designed to maintain a lambda 1 air-fuel ratio throughout its operating range.
As if the aforementioned weren't enough, the engine that will power the Golf R twins from mid-2027 also replaces the conventional alternator and starter motor with a starter-generator thingy that runs on 48 volts. Similar to the T-Roc R, the Golf will continue using a seven-speed tranny of the DCT variety in combination with the R Performance rear torque splitter-type 4MOTION all-wheel-drive system.
While the rear axle may get the same 50 percent torque split as regular 4MOTION, the rear torque splitter sends up to 100 percent of that rear-axle torque to either rear wheel for better cornering. Said rear-axle setup also enables Drift and Nurburgring-focused operating modes.
Drift mode forces 100 percent of the rear axle's torque to the outside rear wheel, overdriving it during a turn to kick out the rear end into a slide. Nurburgring mode, by comparison, maximizes corner-exit speeds by carefully balancing torque between the left and right rear wheels.
